title: I.G., AND OTHERS v. SLOVAKIA
summary: In the case of I.G. and Others v. Slovakia, the applicants—Ms I.G., Ms M.K., and Ms R.H.—are Slovakian nationals of Roma ethnic origin who brought a complaint against Slovakia. The case centres on the profound vulnerability of Roma women subjected to sterilisation without their full and informed consent, a practice that has disproportionately affected Roma and Traveller women in Europe and raises serious concerns about discrimination and bodily autonomy. The applicants were sterilised at Krompachy Hospital during or after childbirth between 1999 and 2000, when two of them were still minors. They allege that they were neither properly informed about the procedure nor gave valid consent, and in some cases only discovered they had been sterilised years later when reviewing their medical records. Despite their complaints, Slovak authorities repeatedly discontinued criminal investigations, concluding that the procedures were medically justified and that consent had been obtained, though the applicants and their representatives strongly disputed this. The European Court of Human Rights declared the case admissible and examined potential violations of Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 8 (right to respect for private and family life), 12 (right to marry and found a family), 13 (right to an effective remedy), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights. While the final judgment on the merits was pending at this stage, the admissibility decision marked a crucial step in recognising the gravity of forced sterilisation claims. This case is significant as it highlights the historical pattern of reproductive rights violations against Roma and Traveller women in Europe, underscoring the need for robust legal protections and accountability.
